title: Alert Fired But No One Can Tell What's Actually Wrong
intro: An Alertmanager alert fired: 'HighErrorRate on checkout-service'. Nobody's sure if it's real or if users are actually affected.

steps.prompt: Check the actual error rate right now, not just trust the alert fired.
steps.hint: Query the exact metric the alert is based on — confirm the number is genuinely elevated, not a stale/flapping alert.

steps.prompt: Check total traffic volume too — a high rate on low traffic can look scarier than it is.
steps.hint: 0.18 errors/sec against 1.2 total requests/sec — do that division: that's roughly 15% error rate, not negligible.

steps.prompt: Check saturation — is the service under resource pressure?
steps.hint: CPU near its limit is a strong saturation signal — check this alongside error rate, not instead of it.

steps.prompt: Pull recent logs to see the actual errors, not just the rate.
steps.fake_output:
ERROR: request queue full, rejecting request
ERROR: request queue full, rejecting request
steps.hint: The actual error message usually tells you which of the four golden signals is the real root cause.

resolution: The service was CPU-saturated (near its limit) and started rejecting requests once its internal queue filled up, which is exactly what the elevated 500 rate was measuring — this wasn't a flaky alert, it was traffic genuinely exceeding capacity. The right response is scaling out (more replicas) or scaling up (higher CPU limit/request), not just 'restarting the pods', since a restart under sustained load just repeats the same saturation shortly after. The deeper lesson: an alert on error rate alone doesn't tell you why — cross-referencing traffic volume, saturation, and logs together (the four golden signals) is what actually diagnoses it.
